clue.text: See subordinate with time for a break learning to earn a crust

indicators.note: breaking a word up lets its letters be put back together in a different order
one thing standing for another means it takes the other's place in the word

parts.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time
the letter that is swapped out

explanation.surface: Someone is told to watch a junior employee who has been given time off for a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the A of SUBORDINATE for T, then rearrange. 'See' just invites the solver to look at the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Brotstudien is German for 'bread studies': study pursued purely as a means of making a living, the bread being one's crust.

clue.text: Intoxicant, heroin taken in injection

indicators.note: something taken in is held inside something else

parts.note: a bang is slang for a shot of a drug
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A drug warning: the heroin was taken by injection.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes inside BANG.
explanation.definitionFit: Bhang is a preparation of cannabis leaves used in India, so it is a drug that intoxicates.

clue.text: Outcry going up about training e.g. falcon

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other
in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a roar is a loud outcry; reading upwards it becomes RAOR
PT is physical training

explanation.surface: People protest loudly about how falcons are trained.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light the reversed outcry reads from the bottom up, and the training abbreviation sits in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A raptor is a bird of prey, and the falcon is one example of the class.

clue.text: Massage auntie endlessly administered

indicators.note: without its end, the word loses its last letter
administered suggests something dispensed or worked over, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: auntie without its final letter

explanation.surface: A relative gives somebody a massage.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuina is a form of Chinese therapeutic massage, so it names a particular kind of rubdown.

clue.text: Being full, here's dish lad's left for particular one?

definitions.note: a participial phrase standing for the adjective

indicators.note: one item left in place of another means it is swapped out for a replacement

parts.note: a salad is a dish
the letters to be swapped out
Ted is one particular lad, a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone has eaten their fill; a dish has been left for one fussy diner.
explanation.walkthrough: In SALAD, the general LAD makes way for a particular lad, TED.
explanation.definitionFit: Sated means having had enough food, the condition of a stomach that is full.

clue.text: Stall, opposite of stand put up and occupied by vicar?

indicators.note: something occupied has another thing sitting inside it
in a down entry, put up means raised so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to sit is the opposite of to stand; read upwards it becomes TIS
Rev, short for Reverend, is a vicar's title

explanation.surface: A church stall that is not for standing is put up and used by the vicar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stall' looks like a verb or a market stand; here it is a Scots noun for a division in a stable.
explanation.definitionFit: Trevis is a Scots word for a partition between stalls in a stable, and by extension a stall itself.

clue.text: Sign of hesitation going over slope of hill in shades

parts.note: um is what people say when they hesitate
brae is Scots for a hillside

explanation.surface: A walker pauses, then crosses the slope of a hill in the shade.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'going over' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Umbrae is the plural of umbra, Latin for shadow, so it means shadows or shades.

clue.text: Scribbled blog in base? Base indeed

indicators.note: scribbled writing is messy, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: Someone writes a scrappy blog post from their base and it is a low act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' appears twice: first as the mathematical base E, then as the definition, hence 'indeed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignoble means dishonourable or mean, exactly the moral sense of base.

clue.text: English Queen about reign formerly: 'My colours will not fade'

indicators.note: about means round the outside, so the pair wraps another piece

parts.note: Eng is the abbreviation for English
R for Regina, queen
raine is Spenser's old spelling of reign

explanation.surface: An English monarch looks back on a past reign and boasts that her flags will never fade.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser's spellings are fair game in Azed, which uses Chambers. The definition is a quotation: what such a dyer might boast of their fast-dyed cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: An engrainer dyes in grain, fixing colour deep in the fibre, so the dye stays fast and does not fade.

clue.text: What may be part of radical combination, ideal for singer?

definitions.text: What may be part of radical combination

parts.note: ace means first-rate, ideal
tone is the quality of voice a singer works on

explanation.surface: A chemist and a singing coach meet: one's radical mix, the other's perfect voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radical' is the chemical sense: a group of atoms behaving as a unit; acetone contains the acetyl-type group and joins such combinations.
explanation.definitionFit: Acetone is an organic solvent and reagent that can bond with chemical radicals, so it can be one component of a compound.

clue.text: Tribal division united by chance

parts.note: hap is an old word for chance or luck
U for united, as in football club names

explanation.surface: A tribe's sections came together by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United by chance' puts U beside HAP, with HAP first.
explanation.definitionFit: A hapu is a Maori sub-tribe, a section within a larger iwi.

clue.text: Strong drink artist tipped over more than half of historical document

indicators.note: something tipped over ends upside down, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the usual artist

indicators.note: only the larger front part of the document's name is kept, the rest cut away

parts.note: the Magna Carta of 1215

explanation.surface: A drunk painter knocks over the Magna Carta.
explanation.walkthrough: Six of the ten letters of MAGNA CARTA count as more than half.
explanation.definitionFit: Armagnac is a brandy from Gascony, a spirit and therefore a strong drink.

clue.text: 'Pale, rocky' encapsulates it

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose, so one piece is held inside the other
rocky means unsteady, so the letters of the word before it wobble out of order

parts.note: taken as written; rearranged as APLE
taken as written

explanation.surface: A summary description of a stone: the words pale and rocky sum it up.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: aplite is a pale rock, and the phrase does describe it.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplite is a light-coloured fine-grained granite, so 'pale' and 'rocky' together capture it.

clue.text: Nick damaged leg in prang on Aussie road

parts.note: the nick and the bin are both slang for a place of confinement

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written; rearranged as GLE

explanation.surface: Nick hurt his leg in a car crash in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a man's name; it is slang. A prang is British slang for a car crash.
explanation.definitionFit: Bingle is Australian slang for a minor road accident, the same thing a Briton calls a prang.

clue.text: Gaucho's requisite, essential to fill a zoo's stock

indicators.note: what is essential to a phrase lies at its core, inside the words

parts.note: found across fiLL A ZOo's
surface padding completing the picture of animals in a zoo

explanation.surface: A cowboy's rope is needed to stock a zoo with animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazo is a lasso, the rope a South American cowboy needs for catching cattle.

clue.text: Underwear of a kind, wedding kit for the groom? (9, two words)

definitions.meaning: second meaning, whimsical: the outfit worn for a marriage, a union

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: a marriage is a union, and a groom wears a suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A union suit is the American name for combinations, one-piece long underwear covering body and legs.

clue.text: Honeyed tipple imbibed by inamorata

indicators.note: what is imbibed sits inside the drinker, so the letters lie within the word

parts.note: found inside inaMORATa

explanation.surface: A sweet drink is sipped by someone's beloved.
explanation.definitionFit: Morat is an old drink of honey flavoured with mulberries, so a sweetened beverage.

clue.text: Sex organ's linga oda exercised!

definitions.note: a possessive standing for an adjective

indicators.note: exercised means put through movements, so the letters are shifted about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a harem room and phallic symbols being worked hard.
explanation.walkthrough: A linga is a phallic emblem of Shiva and an oda a room in a harem, so the surface is suggestive.
explanation.definitionFit: Gonadial is the adjective for gonad, a reproductive gland, so it means belonging to a sex organ.

clue.text: Cramp displayed by 50% of sportsmen?

indicators.note: fifty per cent keeps only half the word and drops the other half

parts.note: cricketers are sportsmen

explanation.surface: Half a team of athletes go down with cramp.
explanation.walkthrough: The first five of the ten letters of CRICKETERS are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A crick is a painful muscle spasm, especially in the neck, much like a cramp.

clue.text: Treats with special care lines of salad crops?

parts.note: cos is a variety of lettuce
sets are rows or lots of young plants set out

explanation.surface: A gardener tends rows of lettuce lovingly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines of salad crops' reads as sets of cos, written COS then SETS.
explanation.definitionFit: To cosset is to pamper someone, giving them special attention and comfort.

clue.text: Coca Cola's half wasted with last of lemonade in the drains

indicators.note: wasted suggests ruined or wrecked, so the letters are thrown into disorder
half of a word keeps only part of it and loses the rest

parts.note: taken as written
its second half is kept

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of lemonade

explanation.surface: Half-drunk fizzy drinks and lemonade are poured away down the sink.
explanation.walkthrough: COCA plus the back half of COLA plus E are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloacae is the plural of cloaca, Latin for a sewer, so it means drains.

clue.text: Circus performer traditionally — a line's juggling round ball (7, two words)

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the letters go about another piece
juggled items fly about, so the letters come down in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
O is round like a ball

explanation.surface: A circus act: a line of performers juggling with a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting for the answer, which classically balances a ball on its nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Sea lions were traditional circus animals, trained to balance balls and perform tricks.

clue.text: I'm surprised to be keeping near drunk as aid to maintaining balance

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it, so these go inside the outer piece

parts.note: oh is an exclamation of surprise
to can mean near or close, as in 'pull the door to'
lit is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Someone is surprised that a nearly drunk person can still keep their balance.
explanation.walkthrough: OH holds TO and LIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Otoliths are small chalky stones in the inner ear that help sense gravity and keep the body balanced.

clue.text: Shift: did Abraham return this after time away?

parts.note: the question asks whether Abraham came back to a place
Ur of the Chaldees was Abraham's birthplace, which he left
surface padding: it explains why he would be returning at all

explanation.surface: A Bible-study question about whether Abraham ever went home after a long absence.
explanation.walkthrough: The question is 'did Abraham return TO UR?': 'this' points at the two words making the answer. Genesis has him leave Ur for Canaan.
explanation.definitionFit: A tour of duty is a spell of work, just as a shift is a period on duty.

clue.text: Verse contest creating excitement I lost?

indicators.note: something lost is gone, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: tension is nervous excitement
the letter removed

explanation.surface: A poetry slam was thrilling, says a competitor who lost.
explanation.walkthrough: TENSION without its I.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenson was a troubadours' poetic debate in which two poets competed in alternating verses.

clue.text: Rising stink left one in a kerfuffle

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: pooh is an exclamation at a bad smell; read upwards it is HOOP
L is the abbreviation for left
a means one

explanation.surface: A growing scandal leaves someone in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stink' looks like a noun for scandal; it is the exclamation one makes at a bad smell, read upwards in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoopla is excited commotion or fuss, the same thing as a kerfuffle.

clue.text: Old couple not active in the household

indicators.note: not means without, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: a ménage is a household
A is the abbreviation for active

explanation.surface: An elderly pair who do little around the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old couple' looks like two pensioners; it is an archaic verb meaning to join. MENAGE loses its A.
explanation.definitionFit: Menge is an obsolete word meaning to mix or mingle, that is to couple things together.

clue.text: Verses composed by young females incorporating literal extremes

indicators.note: incorporating means taking into the body, so the pair goes inside

parts.note: gals are girls
A and Z are the extremes of the alphabet, letters being literals

explanation.surface: Poems written by girls, which include extreme metaphors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literal' is crossword-speak for 'of letters', so the literal extremes are the first and last letters of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A gazal, or ghazal, is a Persian and Urdu form of lyric poem, so gazals are verses.

clue.text: Obscure eon, an age associated with tropical America

indicators.note: to obscure is to muddle, so the letters are hidden in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A forgotten geological era linked to the tropics of the Americas.
explanation.definitionFit: Neogaea is the biogeographical region of the Neotropics, so Neogaean describes things belonging to tropical America.

clue.text: Set about contact sport? It's not very nourishing

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: to gel is to set firm
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A dietitian remarks that a rough team sport is no substitute for a square meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a tennis or kit noun; it is the verb meaning to become firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Gruel is a thin watery porridge, the proverbially meagre food of Victorian workhouses.

clue.text: One against receiving latest bit of advert — it was stuffed under mail

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: receiving means taking something in, so a letter goes inside

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: the latest part of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of advert

explanation.surface: Someone opposed to a leaflet campaign stuffed under the post, or mail, slot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mail' looks like post; it is chain mail armour. CON takes in T, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: An acton was a padded quilted jacket worn under a coat of mail for comfort and protection.

clue.text: After end of monsoon as of old harrow watercourses

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of monsoon
harrow is an old cry of distress, like alas

explanation.surface: After the rains, a field is harrowed beside the streams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harrow' looks like the farm implement; in old usage it is a cry of woe.
explanation.definitionFit: A nala, or nullah, is an Indian word for a stream or ravine that carries water.

clue.text: She's sometimes lazy, coming from the country, opening tin

indicators.note: opening something lets another thing in, so a piece goes inside

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
the USA is the country

explanation.surface: A lazy woman from the countryside opens a can rather than cook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' gives the usual crossword abbreviation for America; 'tin' is its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazy Susan is a revolving tray, so Susan is sometimes paired with lazy in that name.

clue.text: English ploughed furrows, cold inside? Rifts according to the Scots

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: ruts are furrows
C for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A farmer wonders whether the cold has got into the ploughed fields and made cracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rifts' looks like cracks; in Scots and dialect a rift is a belch. C goes inside RUTS, after E.
explanation.definitionFit: To eruct is to belch, which Scots speakers call to rift.

clue.text: Set of bells, including start of octave rings well

indicators.note: including takes something in, so a piece sits inside

parts.note: a peal is a set of bells
ut is the old name of the first note of the scale, now doh

explanation.surface: Church bells start up an octave and ring out well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rings well' looks like praise for the bells; it is the definition, something that encircles a well.
explanation.definitionFit: A puteal is a stone curb or enclosure built round the mouth of a well.

clue.text: Fungicidal compound, litre distributed? I'll have none inserted

indicators.note: inserted means put inside, so one piece goes into the other
distributed things are spread about, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; rearranged as TRILE
azo- comes from Greek a- 'not' and zoe 'life', as in azote, the gas that will not support life

explanation.surface: A drinker refuses any more and pours a litre out.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse of the inserted AZO is a best reading: 'none' as in no life, the Greek root of azote. The rearranged LITRE and the insertion are certain.
explanation.definitionFit: Triazoles are nitrogen ring compounds, many used as agricultural and medical fungicides.

clue.text: Mixed dish to bring on, going round — cut edging off

indicators.note: turning round sends the word back the other way
the edging of a word is its first and last letters, which are cut away

parts.note: to halloo is to urge on hounds with shouts

explanation.surface: A stew is served, passed round and trimmed.
explanation.walkthrough: Reversing gives OOLLAH; trim both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: An olla, as in olla podrida, is a Spanish stew of mixed meats and vegetables.

clue.text: No. 1 in Elysium with threefold head, never dying

definitions.note: a gerund phrase standing for an abstract noun

indicators.note: number one in a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Elysium
ternal means threefold
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: In paradise lives a three-headed creature that never dies.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Cerberus, the three-headed dog at the gates of the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternalness is the state of lasting for ever, the condition of never coming to an end.
